title: The Monty Hall Problem and the Failure of Intuition
question: Why does almost everyone, including many mathematicians, get a simple three-door puzzle wrong?
summary: Switching doors wins two-thirds of the time, yet intuition insists on fifty-fifty. The puzzle reveals that probability is really about information, and that our minds reason poorly about what a revealed fact implies.
content:
The setup

You face three doors: one hides a car, two hide goats. You pick a door. The host, who knows where the car is, opens a different door to reveal a goat and offers you the chance to switch. Should you?

The answer that feels wrong

Switching wins with probability 2/3. Most people reason that two doors remain, so the odds are 50-50. When Marilyn vos Savant published the correct answer in 1990, thousands of readers, including professors, wrote in to say she was mistaken.

Why it works

Your first pick has a 1/3 chance of being right, and nothing the host does can change that, because the host never opens your door and never reveals the car. So the remaining 2/3 is concentrated on the one other closed door. Equivalently: switching wins exactly when your first pick was wrong, which happens 2/3 of the time. With 100 doors, where the host opens 98 goats, the intuition flips instantly.

The hidden assumption

The answer depends on the host's behaviour. If the host opens a random door and merely happens to reveal a goat, switching gives 1/2. The host's knowledge and constraint make the reveal informative. Probability is not about the objects on the table but about the process that generated what you observe.

Why minds resist

We tend to treat the remaining options as equally weighted symmetrical alternatives, ignoring the asymmetry that one door was chosen by us and the other was left by a process that avoids the car. Pigeons, notably, learn to switch faster than humans, apparently because they update on frequencies rather than story-like reasoning.

A broader lesson

The same structure appears in medical testing, courtroom evidence and selection effects. Bayes' theorem is the general rule: update beliefs by how likely the evidence would be under each hypothesis. Monty Hall is a clean laboratory for that principle.

perspectives.title: Mathematics
perspectives.description: Conditional probability and Bayes' theorem give a precise answer: posterior odds depend on the likelihood of the host's action under each scenario.

perspectives.title: Cognitive psychology
perspectives.description: The 50-50 intuition reflects equiprobability bias and difficulty tracking information given by an agent's constrained actions.

perspectives.title: Game theory
perspectives.description: The host is a player with rules, not nature. Changing the host's strategy changes the correct response, so the problem is really about modelling the other agent.

perspectives.title: Education
perspectives.description: Simulation and frequency formats ('imagine 300 games') make the answer intuitive, suggesting how to teach probabilistic reasoning.
